title: Lebanon-Israel Round 3 Day 2 in Washington — Talks Continue as May 17 Ceasefire Expiry Deadline Forces Extension Negotiations; IDF Withdrawal vs. Hezbollah Disarmament Deadlock Persists
detail: The third round of direct Lebanon-Israel negotiations entered its second day at the U.S. State Department on May 15, 2026, with the April 16 ceasefire framework due to expire May 17 — creating acute urgency for a ceasefire extension agreement that would keep diplomatic momentum alive. The Lebanese delegation is led by special envoy Simon Karam with Ambassador Nada Hamadeh Mouawad and a military attaché. The Israeli delegation is led by Ambassador Yechiel Leiter alongside IDF Head of Strategy Brig.-Gen. Amichai Levin, an NSC representative, and a military attaché. The U.S. facilitation team includes Ambassador Mike Huckabee, Ambassador Michael Issa, and Secretary Rubio's adviser Michael Needham, with Secretary Rubio participating directly. Al Jazeera confirmed the talks continued May 15 'as expiration of ceasefire nears.' The fundamental impasse persists: Israel insists on retaining full freedom of military operations in Lebanon until Hezbollah is fully disarmed south of the Litani River — a process Israel does not believe the Lebanese Army can enforce alone; Lebanon insists on an unconditional Israeli withdrawal timetable under UNSC Resolution 1701, with Hezbollah disarmament addressed separately as a Lebanese domestic security matter. The May 17 ceasefire expiry creates two possible outcomes: (1) a framework is agreed to extend the ceasefire, possibly with a phased Israeli withdrawal schedule and strengthened UNIFIL/LAF deployment provisions; (2) the ceasefire lapses with the risk of Lebanon returning to active hostilities. Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem maintains opposition to the Washington direct format, sustaining domestic pressure on PM Nawaf Salam and President Joseph Aoun. The talks represent the most sustained direct diplomatic engagement between Lebanon and Israel since the end of the Lebanese civil war, and the most consequential moment for the Lebanese state's diplomatic strategy in decades.

title: India-Pakistan Backchannel Contacts Continue One Year After Operation Sindoor Ceasefire — Pakistan Signals Openness to Dialogue; Formal Talks Remain Frozen
detail: One year after the U.S.-brokered India-Pakistan ceasefire that ended Operation Sindoor (May 10, 2025), India-Pakistan backchannel contacts continue despite frozen official diplomatic relations. Pakistan's foreign ministry on May 14, 2026 reacted positively to RSS senior official Hosabale's call for resuming India-Pakistan dialogue and sporting ties — a cautious signal that both sides are exploring the political conditions for normalized relations without official bilateral talks. A Washington Post op-ed (May 5, 2026) documented that the ceasefire has held 'so far' — the line of control remains quiet — while at least four back-channel meetings have taken place (two Track 1.5, two Track 2). Pakistan's Army Chief's May 2026 speeches were analyzed by The Diplomat as revealing intentions about the future trajectory of the conflict — suggesting Pakistani military calculus is still evolving. The Friday Times (May 13) described Pakistan as undergoing a 'forced diplomatic and geopolitical reset' that may open space for normalization. Al Jazeera's year-anniversary assessment ('Two wins, two losses: What India and Pakistan have learned a year after war') framed the situation as: India won tactical military credibility; Pakistan won international sympathy; both sides face 'rising risks and deepening instability' without a political resolution. The fundamental issues that drove Operation Sindoor — terrorism support infrastructure allegations, Indus Waters Treaty suspension (India cancelled the treaty April 2025 following the Pahalgam attack that killed 26 civilians), Kashmir status, and LOC normalization — remain unresolved. Formal bilateral talks, summit meetings, and people-to-people exchanges remain suspended. The cautious positive signaling on May 14-15 represents a shift in political rhetoric without a diplomatic framework breakthrough.

media.caption: Washington Post: A year later, India and Pakistan's ceasefire is holding — so far — May 5, 2026
